content: Postpartum endometritis is an infection that occurs when vaginal organisms invade the endometrial cavity during labor. This condition is more frequently observed after cesarean delivery and requires antibiotic treatment. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate treatment failure and complications associated with various antibiotic regimens for postpartum endometritis. The review included 42 randomized trials, with data from 40 trials involving 4,240 participants. Twenty of these studies, encompassing 1,918 women, compared the combination of clindamycin and an aminoglycoside (gentamicin in most studies, with one study using tobramycin) to other antibiotic regimens. When compared to cephalosporins, the combination of clindamycin and an aminoglycoside resulted in fewer treatment failures (relative risk [RR] 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.49 to 0.99; 872 participants; 8 studies; low-quality evidence). Similarly, fewer treatment failures were observed when compared to penicillins (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.90; 689 participants; 7 studies; low-quality evidence). However, for other antibiotic subgroups, such as monobactams and quinolones, the differences in treatment failure rates were not statistically significant. The combination of clindamycin and an aminoglycoside also resulted in significantly fewer wound infections compared to cephalosporins (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.93; 500 participants; 4 studies; low-quality evidence). Additionally, treatment with gentamicin and clindamycin was associated with fewer treatment failures compared to gentamicin and penicillin (RR 2.57, 95% CI 1.48 to 4.46; 200 participants; 1 study). Regimens that included agents with longer half-lives, allowing for less frequent administration, were associated with fewer treatment failures (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.92; 484 participants; 2 studies) compared to regimens using cefoxitin. Conversely, regimens with poor activity against penicillin-resistant anaerobic bacteria were associated with higher rates of treatment failure (RR 1.94, 95% CI 1.38 to 2.72; 774 participants; 7 studies) and wound infections (RR 1.88, 95% CI 1.17 to 3.02; 740 participants; 6 studies) compared to regimens with good activity against these bacteria. Once-daily dosing of antibiotics was associated with a shorter hospital stay (mean difference [MD] -0.73 days, 95% CI -1.27 to -0.20; 322 participants; 3 studies). There were no significant differences between groups in terms of severe complications, and no maternal deaths were reported in any of the trials. Regarding secondary outcomes, three studies compared continued oral antibiotic therapy after intravenous therapy to no oral therapy. These studies found no differences in rates of recurrent endometritis or other outcomes. Additionally, no differences were observed between groups in terms of allergic reactions. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was unclear, and the quality of evidence, as assessed using the GRADE approach, was low to very low for outcomes such as therapeutic failure, severe complications, wound infections, and allergic reactions. In conclusion, the combination of clindamycin and gentamicin is an effective treatment for postpartum endometritis. Regimens with good activity against penicillin-resistant anaerobic bacteria are superior to those with poor activity against these organisms. There is no evidence to suggest that any specific regimen is associated with fewer side effects. Furthermore, after clinical improvement of uncomplicated endometritis treated with intravenous therapy, additional oral antibiotic therapy has not been shown to provide any benefit.
